newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FULL TEXT-Philippine C. Bank peso explanation.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT-Philippine C. Bank peso explanation.

text.p: The following statement given with questions and answers was released by Central Bank governor Gabriel Singson at a news conference.
Q. Why are you devaluing the peso?

A. We are not really devaluing the peso since the peso exchange rate is not fixed to begin with. What we have decided to do is simply allow the peso to move within a new wider range consistent with a market-determined exchange rate policy. This will allow more timely adjustment in light of more difficult conditions prevailing in regional currency markets.
Of course, under current circumstances, this has led to a depreciation of the peso but we expect this temporary situation to stabilise as markets are invariably self-correcting.
Q. What do you hope to achieve with this decision?

A. Our principal concern is to protect the well-earned economic gains of the Filipino people from current turbulence in regional currency markets. A more flexible exchange rate will conserve our international reserves and normalise interest rates to levels compatible with the needs of our fast growing economy. A more flexible exchange rate will also prevent speculators from gaining at the expense of the rest of the economy. .
Q. Is this MB (Monetary Board) decision supported by the President and the Cabinet?
A. Yes. The President has actually issued a statement strongly supporting the Monetary Board's decision.
Q. Is our situation similar to Thailand, which is why we are doing this?

A. No. There are important differences between the Philippines and Thailand. Philippine economic fundamentals remain very strong. Our economic growth is accelerating. Inflation is declining. Our financial system is very healthy. And we are precisely allowing more exchange rate flexibility to preserve all of these gains.
Q. What is the level of reserves today?
A. Our latest estimate is about $10.0 billion.
Q. How will the new approach conserve our international reserves?
A. We don't expect to intervene substantially in the foreign exchange market thereby conserving our international reserves.
Q. Why don't we use all of our international reserves to defend the peso?
A. Our fundamental exchange rate policy is to allow the exchange rate to be determined by market forces. Using up our reserves to go against the market is incompatible with that policy.
Q. At what exchange rate do you expect the market to settle?

A. That is difficult to say as the market basically reflects the collective decision of all the participants and not just the BSP (Central Bank). But you can be sure that we will continue to monitor market developments and ensure orderly market conditions.

If you remember, the peso-dollar exchange rate had fluctuated over the years. For example, in November 1994, the lowest rate of P23.88 = $1 was experienced. In contrast, a high rate of P29.81 = $1 occurred in September 1993.
Q. Where you pressured by the IMF into this decision?

A. No. We can assure you that this was a decision made solely by the Monetary Board. Our track record will show that we have been following an independent monetary and exchange rate policy course which we believe are in the country's best interests.
Q. Will this affect our IMF exit program?
A. By allowing us to preserve the economic gains we have already achieved, this will further enhance our capacity to exit from the IMF on a very sound economic footing.
Q. What will be the effect of this new approach on inflation? Interest rates? Government revenues? Prices?
A. In the long run, by allowing the economy to continue to sustain its growth and productive capacity, inflation and interest rates will decline, and government revenues will improve.
